questions.question: How does Python resolve a variable name?
questions.title: Python LEGB Scope Rule
questions.direct_answer: Python searches for a name in Local, Enclosing-function, Global, then Built-in scope—the LEGB rule. Use nonlocal to rebind an enclosing variable and global only when a function must rebind a module-level name.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand nested functions, closures, and shadowing.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming assignment automatically updates a global or enclosing variable.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that assignment makes a name local unless global or nonlocal declares otherwise.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define Python LEGB Scope Rule simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: LEGB lookup
sections.content: Python resolves reads from the nearest scope outward: Local, Enclosing, Global, and Built-in. Assignment inside a function creates a local name by default.

sections.title: nonlocal rebinding
sections.content:
```python
def counter():
    n = 0
    def next_value():
        nonlocal n
        n += 1
        return n
    return next_value
```

sections.title: Interview cues
items: Assignment defaults to the local scope.
Prefer passing values and returning results over global state.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Python uses the LEGB rule: Local, Enclosing, Global, and Built-in. A function assignment is local unless I explicitly use nonlocal or global, so I prefer explicit parameters and return values to avoid hidden state.

sections.title: Concept explained
sections.content: Walk through the example step by step, then say when this approach is a good fit and what you would test at the boundary.
